## RQ1 - Differential expression

Loading the IMvigor210 data and preparing it for analysis by removing the genes without a valid name, checking that the clinical table matches the expression columns, filtering out genes with very low counts, and normalizing the data with a variance-stabilizing transformation so that samples can be compared fairly.

```{r}
# Use whichever copy of the dataset exists on this machine, so the document
# runs unchanged on the server and on each of our laptops.
data_paths <- c(
  "/home/projects/22123/IMvigor210_plain.rds",              # teaching server
  "/Users/vvtch/Downloads/IMvigor210.rds",                  # Vera
  "/Users/dhruva/Downloads/IMvigor210_plain - Copy.rds"     # Dhruva
)
data_path <- data_paths[file.exists(data_paths)][1]
if (is.na(data_path)) stop("IMvigor210 dataset not found. Add your path to data_paths.")
cat("Loading:", data_path, "\n")

data <- readRDS(data_path)
counts <- data[["counts"]]
tpm <- data[["tpm"]]
clinical <- data[["clinical"]]

dim(counts); dim(tpm); str(clinical)

filter <- dplyr::filter

starfish      <- as.character(pnw_palette("Starfish", 7, type = "discrete"))
starfish_cont <- as.character(pnw_palette("Starfish", 100, type = "continuous"))
col_BOR       <- c(NR = starfish[2], R = starfish[6])   
set.seed(42)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

```{r}
ok_genes <- !is.na(rownames(counts)) & rownames(counts) != ""
counts   <- counts[ok_genes, ]
tpm      <- tpm[rownames(tpm) %in% rownames(counts), ]


sum(duplicated(rownames(counts)))

# DESeq2 needs integer counts
all(counts == round(counts))

coldata <- as.data.frame(clinical)
rownames(coldata) <- coldata$sample_id
coldata <- coldata[colnames(counts), ]                 
stopifnot(all(rownames(coldata) == colnames(counts)))  


coldata$BOR <- factor(coldata$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R"))
table(coldata$BOR, useNA = "ifany")
summary(coldata$TMB)


sample_id <- colnames(counts)[10]
sample_id %in% colnames(tpm)

df_sample <- data.frame(
  counts = counts[, sample_id],
  tpm    = tpm[, sample_id]
)

p1 <- ggplot(df_sample, aes(x = counts)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = starfish[3], color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Raw counts", subtitle = sample_id, x = "Raw count", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

p2 <- ggplot(df_sample, aes(x = log2(counts + 1))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = starfish[2], color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "log2(counts + 1)", subtitle = sample_id, x = "log2(count + 1)", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

p3 <- ggplot(df_sample, aes(x = tpm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = starfish[3], color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "TPM", subtitle = sample_id, x = "TPM", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

p4 <- ggplot(df_sample, aes(x = log2(tpm + 1))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = starfish[2], color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "log2(TPM + 1)", subtitle = sample_id, x = "log2(TPM + 1)", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)
```

```{r}
lib_df <- data.frame(sample = colnames(counts), lib_size = colSums(counts) / 1e6)

ggplot(lib_df, aes(x = lib_size)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = starfish[4], color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Library size (millions of reads)", y = "Number of samples") +

```

```{r}
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts,
                              colData   = coldata,
                              design    = ~ BOR)

n_before <- nrow(dds)
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10
dds  <- dds[keep, ]
cat("Genes before filtering:", n_before, "| after:", nrow(dds), "\n")
```

```{r}
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)

pca_df <- plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "BOR", returnData = TRUE)
percent_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_df, "percentVar"), 1)

pca_df$TMB      <- coldata[pca_df$name, "TMB"]
pca_df$lib_size <- colSums(counts(dds))[pca_df$name] / 1e6

p_pca_bor <- ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = BOR)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_BOR) +
  labs(title = "PCA (vst) coloured by response",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", percent_var[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", percent_var[2], "%)"),
       color = "Response") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

p_pca_tmb <- ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = log2(TMB + 1))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = starfish_cont, na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(title = "PCA (vst) coloured by TMB",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", percent_var[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", percent_var[2], "%)"),
       color = "log2(TMB + 1)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)

grid.arrange(p_pca_bor, p_pca_tmb, ncol = 2)
ggsave("figures/RQ1_pca_response_tmb.png",
       arrangeGrob(p_pca_bor, p_pca_tmb, ncol = 2), width = 11, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

The PCA shows that responders and non-responders overlap almost completely along PC1 (17.7% of variance) and PC2 (10.8%), and TMB shows no gradient along either axis (grey points are the 42 samples without TMB). The main sources of variation in the data are therefore not response or TMB, and the difference between responders and non-responders is subtle enough that it has to be found with gene-level differential expression testing. The samples form one continuous cloud with no clear outliers, so none were removed.

```{r}
ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, color = lib_size)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = starfish_cont) +
  labs(title = "PCA (vst) coloured by library size", color = "Library size (M)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)
```

```{r}
top500  <- head(order(rowVars(assay(vsd)), decreasing = TRUE), 500)
pca_all <- prcomp(t(assay(vsd)[top500, ]))

pc_df <- data.frame(pca_all$x[, 1:5], BOR = vsd$BOR) |>
  pivot_longer(-BOR, names_to = "PC", values_to = "score")

ggplot(pc_df, aes(BOR, score, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ PC, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_BOR) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none")

pc_df |> group_by(PC) |>
  summarise(p = wilcox.test(score ~ BOR)$p.value) |>
  mutate(padj = p.adjust(p, method = "BH"))
```

Comparing the R vs NR using DESeq2 to identify genes significantly different among the groups.  

```{r}
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds) 

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("BOR", "R", "NR"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)

res_shr <- lfcShrink(dds, contrast = c("BOR", "R", "NR"), res = res, type = "normal")
res_df <- as.data.frame(res_shr) |>
  rownames_to_column("gene") |>
  mutate(direction = case_when(
    !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange >  1 ~ "Up in R",
    !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "Up in NR",
    TRUE ~ "Not significant"))

table(res_df$direction)


res_df |> filter(direction != "Not significant") |> arrange(padj) |>
  write_csv("RQ1_DE_genes_significant.csv")
```

Gene set enrichment analysis shows which pathways are higher in responders or non-responders, telling what the differentially expressed genes do, which then relates to how the immune system responds to immunotherapy.

```{r}
top_label <- res_df |> filter(direction != "Not significant") |>
  arrange(padj) |> head(15)

p_volcano <- ggplot(res_df |> filter(!is.na(padj)),
                    aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), color = direction)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_text_repel(data = top_label, aes(label = gene), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Up in R" = col_BOR[["R"]], "Up in NR" = col_BOR[["NR"]],
                                "Not significant" = "grey75")) +
  labs(title = "Volcano plot: R vs NR",
       x = "Shrunken log2 fold change (R vs NR)",
       y = "-log10 adjusted p-value", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_volcano
ggsave("figures/RQ1_volcano.png", p_volcano, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

The volcano plot shows a modest set of differentially expressed genes. The strongest genes reach an adjusted p-value of about 10^-8. More genes are higher in non-responders (left) than in responders (right).

The responder side includes immune-related genes such as CCL5, a chemokine that recruits T cells, and ZNF683, a marker of tissue-resident cytotoxic T cells. This fits the idea that responders have a more inflamed, T-cell-rich tumour. The non-responder side is dominated by epithelial and tumour-type genes (MUC6, PAX8, MMP7, TCN1, CP, C9, SERPINA5). MMP7 also points to tissue remodelling, which is consistent with a tumour environment that is less immune-active. The shrunken fold changes are mostly between 1 and 4, so the effects are moderate. With only 25 responders, power is limited, and the list should be seen as suggestive. The plot only shows association, not whether these genes cause the response.

```{r}
top_genes <- res_df |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> arrange(padj) |> head(40) |> pull(gene)

mat <- t(scale(t(assay(vsd)[top_genes, ])))          # z-score per gene

annot <- data.frame(BOR = colData(vsd)$BOR,
                    TMB = colData(vsd)$TMB,
                    row.names = colnames(vsd))

pheatmap(mat, annotation_col = annot, show_colnames = FALSE,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         color = starfish_cont,
         annotation_colors = list(BOR = col_BOR, TMB = starfish_cont),
         main = "Top 40 DE genes (vst, row z-score)")

pheatmap(mat, annotation_col = annot, show_colnames = FALSE,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2",
         color = starfish_cont,
         annotation_colors = list(BOR = col_BOR, TMB = starfish_cont),
         main = "Top 40 DE genes (vst, row z-score)",
         filename = "figures/RQ1_heatmap_top40.png", width = 8, height = 9)
```

```{r}
             fgsea_hallmark = fgsea_hallmark),
        "RQ1_objects.rds")


```

Differences in expression can be influenced by confounding factors such as tumour mutational burden, sample quality and tumour purity. Also, a gene that is differentially expressed is only associated with response; this does not show that the gene causes the response.

## RQ2 — Immune-related signatures

Is the 18-gene T-cell–inflamed GEP (Ayers et al. 2017, [10.1172/JCI91190](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI91190)) associated with response to anti-PD-L1 treatment?

### Data and the published gene set

We use `log2(TPM + 1)`: z-scoring later cancels gene length, but not per-sample sequencing depth, which TPM corrects and raw counts do not.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-setup

# Reuses `tpm` and `clinical` loaded in RQ1.
clinical_rq2 <- as.data.frame(clinical)

# Align clinical rows to expression columns before anything else.
id_col <- if ("sample_id" %in% names(clinical_rq2)) "sample_id" else "pat_id"
clinical_rq2 <- clinical_rq2[match(colnames(tpm), clinical_rq2[[id_col]]), ]
stopifnot(identical(as.character(clinical_rq2[[id_col]]), colnames(tpm)))

clinical_rq2$BOR <- factor(clinical_rq2$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R"))
table(clinical_rq2$BOR, useNA = "ifany")

log_tpm_rq2 <- log2(as.matrix(tpm) + 1)

# Project palette (from Q1) and the AUC helper, both used throughout RQ2.
bor_cols <- col_BOR

# AUC via the Mann-Whitney identity: P(responder scores above non-responder),
# ties counted as half.
auc_mw <- function(score, pos) {
  comp <- outer(score[pos], score[!pos], "-")
  mean((comp > 0) + 0.5 * (comp == 0))
}
```

The 18 genes of the T-cell-inflamed GEP, as listed in the course exercise.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-genes

# The 18-gene list as given in the course exercise (Exercise 6).
gep_genes <- c(
  "CD27", "CD274", "PDCD1", "CD276", "CD8A", "CMKLR1",
  "CXCL9", "CXCR6", "HLA-DQA1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E",
  "IDO1", "LAG3", "NKG7", "PDCD1LG2", "PSMB10", "STAT1", "TIGIT"
)
stopifnot(length(gep_genes) == 18)

gep_present <- intersect(gep_genes, rownames(log_tpm_rq2))
gep_missing <- setdiff(gep_genes, rownames(log_tpm_rq2))

cat("GEP genes found:", length(gep_present), "of 18\n")
if (length(gep_missing)) cat("Missing:", paste(gep_missing, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

### Expression of the 18 genes in this cohort

Median expression and detection rate per gene, to catch any that are too sparsely measured to contribute.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-gene-summary

gep_mat <- log_tpm_rq2[gep_present, , drop = FALSE]

gene_summary <- data.frame(
  gene       = rownames(gep_mat),
  median_log2tpm = apply(gep_mat, 1, median),
  iqr_log2tpm    = apply(gep_mat, 1, IQR),
  pct_detected   = 100 * rowMeans(tpm[gep_present, , drop = FALSE] > 0)
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(median_log2tpm))

gene_summary
```

*All 18 genes are present, but `HLA-DQA1` is detected in only a third of samples and will carry little information.*

Per-gene association with response, BH-corrected within the 18 genes only. RQ1's genome-wide DESeq2 is the stricter test, printed alongside for contrast.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-per-gene

resp <- clinical_rq2$BOR == "R"

per_gene <- data.frame(
  gene      = rownames(gep_mat),
  median_NR = apply(gep_mat[, !resp, drop = FALSE], 1, median),
  median_R  = apply(gep_mat[,  resp, drop = FALSE], 1, median),
  auc       = apply(gep_mat, 1, auc_mw, pos = resp),
  p         = apply(gep_mat, 1, function(v) wilcox.test(v ~ clinical_rq2$BOR)$p.value)
)
per_gene$padj <- p.adjust(per_gene$p, method = "BH")
per_gene <- per_gene[order(per_gene$p), ]

print(per_gene, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
cat("\nSignificant within the signature (BH, 18 tests):",
    sum(per_gene$padj < 0.05), "of", nrow(per_gene), "\n")

# The same genes under RQ1's genome-wide DESeq2 model, for contrast.
if (exists("res")) {
  deseq_18 <- as.data.frame(res[rownames(gep_mat), c("log2FoldChange", "padj")])
  cat("Significant genome-wide (DESeq2, Q1):",
      sum(deseq_18$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), "of", nrow(deseq_18), "\n")
  print(round(deseq_18[order(deseq_18$padj), ], 4))
}
```

*15 of the 18 genes are individually associated with response; the exceptions are `HLA-DQA1`, `CD276` and `HLA-DRB1`.*

```{r}
#| label: rq2-gene-boxplots
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

# as_tibble keeps non-syntactic gene names such as HLA-DQA1 intact.
gep_long <- tibble::as_tibble(t(gep_mat), rownames = "sample") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-sample, names_to = "gene", values_to = "log2tpm") |>
  dplyr::mutate(BOR = clinical_rq2$BOR[match(sample, colnames(gep_mat))])

p_rq2_genes <- ggplot(gep_long, aes(x = BOR, y = log2tpm, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.4, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y", ncol = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = bor_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression of the 18 T-cell-inflamed GEP genes by response",
    x = NULL, y = expression(log[2]*"(TPM + 1)"), fill = "Response"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p_rq2_genes
ggsave("figures/RQ2_gene_boxplots.png", p_rq2_genes, width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

Spearman correlations between the 18 genes. Co-variation means they measure one underlying phenotype, so averaging should reduce noise; whether the average beats a single gene is tested separately below.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-coexpression
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6

gep_cor <- cor(t(gep_mat), method = "spearman")

cat("Mean pairwise Spearman correlation:",
    round(mean(gep_cor[lower.tri(gep_cor)]), 3), "\n")

pheatmap(
  gep_cor,
  breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 101),
  color = starfish_cont,
  clustering_method = "ward.D2",
  main = "Co-expression of GEP genes (Spearman)"
)

pheatmap(
  gep_cor, breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 101), color = starfish_cont,
  clustering_method = "ward.D2", main = "Co-expression of GEP genes (Spearman)",
  filename = "figures/RQ2_coexpression.png", width = 7, height = 6
)
```

*Mean pairwise ρ = 0.55 and two thirds of pairs exceed 0.5, so the genes largely track one phenotype. `CD276` and `HLA-DQA1` sit outside it.*

### Calculating a GEP score per patient

Z-score each gene across the 192 samples, then average, so every gene contributes equally rather than in proportion to its variance. This is an unweighted simplification of the published NanoString score, so our values rank patients within this cohort but do not match published cut-offs.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-score

gep_z <- t(scale(t(gep_mat)))            # z-score each gene across samples
gep_score <- colMeans(gep_z, na.rm = TRUE)

stopifnot(identical(names(gep_score), colnames(tpm)))

df_rq2 <- data.frame(
  sample    = colnames(tpm),
  gep_score = as.numeric(gep_score),
  BOR       = clinical_rq2$BOR
)

summary(df_rq2$gep_score)
```

### Association between GEP score and response

Wilcoxon rank-sum first: non-parametric, so it suits the unequal groups (25 vs 167) and assumes no normality.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-wilcox

gep_test <- wilcox.test(gep_score ~ BOR, data = df_rq2)
gep_test

aggregate(gep_score ~ BOR, data = df_rq2, FUN = median)
```

*Responders score higher than non-responders (p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴): the association is present.*

For reference, Ayers et al. report AUC = 0.75 for the published weighted GEP score in their own cohort (Figure 4B), against 0.65 for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry.

Logistic regression gives an odds ratio per standard deviation, which is interpretable even though the score has no natural units.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-logistic

df_rq2$gep_sd <- as.numeric(scale(df_rq2$gep_score))

fit_gep <- glm(BOR ~ gep_sd, data = df_rq2, family = binomial)
summary(fit_gep)

# Odds ratio per 1 SD increase in GEP score, with 95% CI.
data.frame(
  OR       = exp(coef(fit_gep))[["gep_sd"]],
  CI_lower = exp(confint.default(fit_gep))["gep_sd", 1],
  CI_upper = exp(confint.default(fit_gep))["gep_sd", 2],
  p_value  = summary(fit_gep)$coefficients["gep_sd", 4]
)
```

*Each standard deviation of score corresponds to 2.3-fold higher odds of complete response.*

AUC is the probability that a random responder outranks a random non-responder, where 0.5 is random ranking.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-auc

is_r <- df_rq2$BOR == "R"
auc_gep <- auc_mw(df_rq2$gep_score, is_r)

# With only 25 responders the AUC is imprecise, so report an interval.
# Stratified bootstrap: resample responders and non-responders separately so
# every replicate keeps the observed 25/167 split.
set.seed(42)
boot_auc <- replicate(2000, {
  idx <- c(sample(which(is_r),  sum(is_r),  replace = TRUE),
           sample(which(!is_r), sum(!is_r), replace = TRUE))
  auc_mw(df_rq2$gep_score[idx], is_r[idx])
})
auc_ci <- quantile(boot_auc, c(0.025, 0.975))

cat("AUC:", round(auc_gep, 3),
    " 95% CI:", paste(round(auc_ci, 3), collapse = " - "), "\n")
```

*AUC 0.733, so discrimination is moderate: clearly better than chance, but one pair in four is still ranked the wrong way round.*

```{r}
  data.frame(

})
```

Split patients by GEP tertile and compare the observed response rate in each.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-tertiles

df_rq2$gep_tertile <- cut(
  df_rq2$gep_score,
  breaks = quantile(df_rq2$gep_score, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
  labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

tertile_tab <- table(df_rq2$gep_tertile, df_rq2$BOR)
tertile_tab

rate_df <- as.data.frame.matrix(tertile_tab) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("gep_tertile") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    n = NR + R,
    response_rate = 100 * R / n,
    gep_tertile = factor(gep_tertile, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  )
rate_df

# Wilson confidence intervals for each tertile's response rate.
wilson <- function(x, n, conf = 0.95) {
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - conf) / 2); ph <- x / n
  cent <- (ph + z^2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  halfw <- z * sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  c(lo = 100 * (cent - halfw), hi = 100 * (cent + halfw))
}
rate_df <- cbind(rate_df, t(mapply(wilson, rate_df$R, rate_df$n)))
rate_df

# Is the response rate monotonically increasing across tertiles?
# prop.trend.test is the trend test; it uses all three groups.
prop.trend.test(rate_df$R, rate_df$n)

# Secondary, post-hoc contrast of the two extreme tertiles only (not a trend
# test, and it discards the middle group). Cutpoints are data-derived.
fisher.test(tertile_tab[c("Low", "High"), ])
```

*Response rate rises monotonically across tertiles, from 4.7% to 25.0% (trend p = 6.4 × 10⁻⁴).*

### Dependence on the weakest genes

Two genes look like dead weight: `HLA-DQA1` is undetected in two thirds of samples, and `CD276` points the opposite way to the rest, which Ayers et al. also report. Our unweighted mean keeps the first and adds the second positively; does either cost anything?

```{r}
#| label: rq2-robustness

score_variant <- function(genes, flip = character()) {
  z <- t(scale(t(log_tpm_rq2[genes, , drop = FALSE])))
  if (length(flip)) z[flip, ] <- -z[flip, ]
  colMeans(z, na.rm = TRUE)
}

variants <- list(
  "all 18 (as published)"        = score_variant(gep_present),
  "drop HLA-DQA1"                = score_variant(setdiff(gep_present, "HLA-DQA1")),
  "CD276 sign-flipped"           = score_variant(gep_present, flip = "CD276"),
  "drop HLA-DQA1 + flip CD276"   = score_variant(setdiff(gep_present, "HLA-DQA1"),
                                                 flip = "CD276")
)

do.call(rbind, lapply(names(variants), function(nm) {
  v <- variants[[nm]]
  data.frame(
    variant    = nm,
    auc        = round(auc_mw(v, is_r), 3),
    wilcox_p   = signif(wilcox.test(v ~ df_rq2$BOR)$p.value, 3),
    cor_to_full = round(cor(v, variants[[1]], method = "spearman"), 3)
  )
}))
```

*No variant moves the AUC by more than 0.005, so the score tolerates its weakest members.*

### Value of the composite over its parts

`CXCL9` alone scores higher than the 18-gene average, so two things need checking: whether that gap exceeds sampling noise, and whether the signature's particular genes matter or any 18 expressed genes would score as well.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-composite

# (a) Composite vs. its best single member.
# The best gene is picked after seeing all 18 results, so this comparison is
# biased in its favour; the confidence interval is the informative part.
best_gene <- per_gene$gene[which.max(per_gene$auc)]
cat("Best single gene:", best_gene, "- AUC", round(max(per_gene$auc), 3),
    "| composite AUC", round(auc_gep, 3), "\n")

set.seed(42)
boot_diff <- replicate(2000, {
  idx <- c(sample(which(is_r),  sum(is_r),  replace = TRUE),
           sample(which(!is_r), sum(!is_r), replace = TRUE))
  auc_mw(df_rq2$gep_score[idx], is_r[idx]) -
    auc_mw(gep_mat[best_gene, idx], is_r[idx])
})
cat("AUC difference (composite - best gene):", round(mean(boot_diff), 3),
    " 95% CI:", paste(round(quantile(boot_diff, c(0.025, 0.975)), 3),
                      collapse = " to "), "\n")

# (b) Composite vs. 18 random expressed genes, scored identically.
# If an arbitrary 18-gene average does as well, the signature is not
# contributing anything specific.
expressed <- rownames(log_tpm_rq2)[rowMeans(tpm > 0) > 0.5 &
                                   apply(log_tpm_rq2, 1, sd) > 0]
set.seed(42)
null_auc <- replicate(1000, {
  g <- sample(expressed, 18)
  auc_mw(colMeans(t(scale(t(log_tpm_rq2[g, , drop = FALSE])))), is_r)
})

cat("\nRandom 18-gene sets (n = 1000): median AUC", round(median(null_auc), 3),
    "| 95th percentile", round(quantile(null_auc, 0.95), 3), "\n")
cat("P(random set >= GEP):", mean(null_auc >= auc_gep), "\n")
```

*`CXCL9` alone is numerically better but not significantly so, and no random 18-gene set reaches the GEP's AUC.*

### Cross-validated discrimination

The score is fixed in advance and not derived from this data, so it cannot overfit; the logistic models can, so we estimate their optimism with repeated stratified 5-fold CV. `mc_sd` measures how stable the CV procedure is; the uncertainty in the AUC itself is the bootstrap interval above.

```{r}
#| label: rq2-cv

auc_cv <- function(dat, form, k = 5, reps = 50) {
  y <- dat$BOR == "R"
  aucs <- numeric(reps)
  for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
    set.seed(r)
    fold <- integer(nrow(dat))
    fold[y]  <- sample(rep_len(1:k, sum(y)))      # stratify so every fold
    fold[!y] <- sample(rep_len(1:k, sum(!y)))     # keeps the event rate
    pred <- numeric(nrow(dat))
    for (i in seq_len(k)) {
      m <- glm(form, data = dat[fold != i, ], family = binomial)
      pred[fold == i] <- predict(m, newdata = dat[fold == i, ], type = "link")
    }
    aucs[r] <- auc_mw(pred, y)                    # pooled out-of-fold AUC
  }
  # SD across repeats = Monte-Carlo noise of the CV procedure itself,
  # NOT sampling uncertainty in the AUC. The bootstrap CI above is that.
  c(cv_auc = mean(aucs), mc_sd = sd(aucs))
}

cv_models <- list(
  "GEP" = list(data.frame(BOR = df_rq2$BOR,
                          gep = as.numeric(scale(df_rq2$gep_score))),
               BOR ~ gep)
)

do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cv_models), function(nm) {
  dat  <- cv_models[[nm]][[1]]
  form <- cv_models[[nm]][[2]]
  ins  <- auc_mw(predict(glm(form, data = dat, family = binomial), type = "link"),
                 dat$BOR == "R")
  cv   <- auc_cv(dat, form)
  data.frame(model     = nm,
             n         = nrow(dat),
             in_sample = round(ins, 3),
             cv_auc    = round(cv[["cv_auc"]], 3),
             mc_sd     = round(cv[["mc_sd"]], 3),
             optimism  = round(ins - cv[["cv_auc"]], 3))
}))
```

*Cross-validated AUC 0.720 against 0.733 in sample, so the optimism is small and the discrimination is real.*

### Interpretation

All 18 genes are present. The score is clearly associated with response: median -0.111 (NR) vs 0.596 (R), Wilcoxon *W* = 1115, *p* = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴; OR 2.34 per SD (95% CI 1.48-3.72); AUC 0.733 (95% CI 0.624-0.831, 0.720 cross-validated); response rate rising 4.7% → 9.4% → 25.0% across tertiles (trend *p* = 6.4 × 10⁻⁴).

Ayers et al. report AUC 0.75 for their weighted score. Ours is consistent with that, though within a wide interval, against a different endpoint (theirs includes partial responses), and without their fitted weights. At most this shows the signature carries real signal in a setting it was not developed for, which is a weaker claim than reproducing their result.

The signature behaves as a unit: mean pairwise ρ = 0.55, and 15 of 18 genes are individually significant (BH within the 18; RQ1's genome-wide DESeq2 is stricter). Strongest are `CXCL9` (0.771), `NKG7` (0.761), `STAT1` (0.760), `LAG3` (0.747). Three contribute nothing: `HLA-DQA1` (detected in 33% of samples), `CD276` (AUC 0.445, the one gene Ayers report as not positively associated with response) and `HLA-DRB1`. Dropping or flipping them moves the AUC only to 0.737, so the average is forgiving of bad members.

We test the composite directly. `CXCL9` alone scores higher (0.771 vs 0.733), but the difference is not significant (−0.039, CI −0.081 to +0.006) and `CXCL9` is a post-hoc winner from 18. Against 1000 random 18-gene sets (median AUC 0.567), none reached the GEP's AUC.

### Biological reading

The GEP summarises the IFN-γ-driven inflamed phenotype across four modules: antigen presentation (`HLA-DQA1`, `HLA-DRB1`, `HLA-E`, `PSMB10`), T-cell recruitment (`CXCL9`, `CXCR6`, `CMKLR1`), cytotoxic activity (`CD8A`, `NKG7`), and adaptive immune resistance, where the IFN-γ signal that attracts T cells also induces the checkpoints restraining them (`PDCD1`, `CD274`, `PDCD1LG2`, `IDO1`, `LAG3`, `TIGIT`). A high score describes a tumour the immune system has already entered and whose brakes are engaged locally, which is the setting where releasing the PD-1/PD-L1 brake has something to act on.

The score is also near-independent of TMB, as RQ3 shows. TMB reports antigenic potential while the GEP reports whether a response materialised, so neither implies the other.

### Why a high GEP score does not guarantee response

AUC 0.73 means roughly one pair in four is ranked wrongly, and three quarters of top-tertile patients still failed to respond. A high score makes response more likely without making it probable.

-   The score cannot see where the T cells are. Mariathasan et al. showed TGF-β-rich stroma confines T cells to the tumour periphery, and bulk RNA-seq cannot separate an infiltrated tumour from an excluded one. Both score high; only one responds.
-   PD-L1 is one brake among several. Resistance also runs through TGF-β, other checkpoints, Tregs and myeloid suppression, loss of antigen presentation (B2M, JAK/STAT), or WNT/β-catenin exclusion.
-   An inflamed tumour still needs something to recognise. Independence from TMB means a high-GEP tumour can carry few neoantigens.
-   The score is cohort-relative. Z-scoring within these 192 patients gives a ranking within the cohort, so published cut-offs do not apply.
-   The genes are not tumour-specific. Expression is diluted by how much immune and stromal tissue the biopsy contained, which is the purity problem taken up in RQ4.
-   The endpoint is the easiest contrast: complete response against progressive disease, 25 responders, intermediates excluded. Discrimination across the full spectrum would be weaker.

## RQ3 — Biomarker comparison

How do PD-1 (PDCD1) expression, immune-related gene signatures, and tumor mutational burden (TMB) compare in their association with different treatment responses? 

```{r}
all(clinical$pat_id %in% colnames(tpm))

# Reorder expression columns to match the phenotype table.
tpm_counts <- tpm[, match(clinical$pat_id, colnames(tpm)), drop = FALSE]

# Explicitly verify the resulting sample order.
stopifnot(identical(clinical$pat_id, colnames(tpm_counts)))

print(table(clinical$BOR, useNA = "ifany"))

# Tumor mutational burden
TMB <- clinical$TMB

# Extract PDCD1 expression.
"PDCD1" %in% rownames(tpm_counts)
PD1 <- as.numeric(log2(tpm_counts["PDCD1", ] + 1))

GEP_genes <- c(
  "CD27", "CD274", "PDCD1", "CD276", "CD8A", "CMKLR1",
  "CXCL9", "CXCR6", "HLA-DQA1", "HLA-DRB1", "HLA-E",
  "IDO1", "LAG3", "NKG7", "PDCD1LG2", "PSMB10", "STAT1", "TIGIT"
)

GEP_genes_present <- GEP_genes[GEP_genes %in% rownames(tpm_counts)]
GEP_genes_missing <- setdiff(GEP_genes, rownames(tpm_counts))

cat("GEP genes present:", length(GEP_genes_present), "of", length(GEP_genes), "\n")
# All 18 present

# Exclude PDCD1 to avoid comparing it against a signature containing itself.
GEP_genes_present <- setdiff(GEP_genes_present, "PDCD1")

# Extract normalized GEP expression.
GEP_counts <- log2(tpm_counts[GEP_genes_present, , drop = FALSE] + 1)

# Standardize each gene across samples.
# scale() operates on columns, so transpose before and after scaling.
GEP_counts_scaled <- t(scale(t(GEP_counts)))

# Average standardized expression across GEP genes for each sample.
GEP_scores <- colMeans(GEP_counts_scaled, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Visualize the distribution of each biomarker in responders and non-responders using boxplots.

Perform appropriate statistical tests to investigate whether each biomarker differs significantly between response groups.

```{r}
plot_Response_boxplot <- function(data, variable, y_label, test_result) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = Response, y = .data[[variable]])) +

    ) +

    ) +

}
```

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  sample = clinical$pat_id,
  TMB = TMB,
  PD1 = PD1,
  GEP_scores = GEP_scores,
  Response = factor(clinical$BOR))

stopifnot(identical(df$sample, colnames(tpm_counts)))
```

Compare the direction and magnitude of the observed differences, and discuss which biomarkers show stronger associations with treatment response.

```{r}
TMB_Response_test <- wilcox.test(TMB ~ Response, data = df)
PD1_Response_test <- wilcox.test(PD1 ~ Response, data = df)
GEP_Response_test <- wilcox.test(GEP_scores ~ Response, data = df)

TMB_Response_test # W = 564.5, p-value = 1.73e-05
PD1_Response_test # W = 1169, p-value = 0.0003961
GEP_Response_test # W = 1122, p-value = 0.0001961

aggregate(
  cbind(TMB, PD1, GEP_scores) ~ Response,
  data = df,
  median
)

kendall_results <- lapply(c("TMB", "PD1", "GEP_scores"), function(v) {
  test <- cor.test(
    df[[v]],
    as.numeric(df$Response == "R"),
    method = "kendall",
    exact = FALSE
  )

  data.frame(
    Biomarker = v,
    Kendall_tau = unname(test$estimate),
    p_value = test$p.value
  )
})

do.call(rbind, kendall_results)
TMB_plot <- plot_Response_boxplot(df, 
                                  "TMB", 
                                  "Tumor mutational burden", 
                                  TMB_Response_test)

PD1_plot <- plot_Response_boxplot(df, 
                                  "PD1", 
                                  "PDCD1 expression", 
                                  PD1_Response_test)

GEP_plot <- plot_Response_boxplot(df, 
                                  "GEP_scores", 
                                  "T cell–inflamed GEP score", 
                                  GEP_Response_test)

grid.arrange(TMB_plot, PD1_plot, GEP_plot, ncol = 3)
```

Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to compare biomarker distributions between responders (R) and non-responders (NR). This non-parametric test is appropriate because the two response groups are independent, their sizes are unequal (25 responders and 167 non-responders, or 21 and 129 for TMB, where 42 patients have no measurement), and it does not require the biomarker values to follow a normal distribution.

All three biomarkers showed statistically significant differences between response groups (p \< 0.001), with higher median values in responders. TMB increased from 7 in non-responders to 14 in responders, PDCD1 expression from 0.55 to 1.2, and the GEP score from -0.15 to 0.55.

Kendall's rank correlation was used to assess the direction and strength of the association between each biomarker and treatment response. This method is suitable because response is a binary variable (NR or R), and it does not assume a linear relationship or normally distributed biomarker values.

All three biomarkers showed statistically significant positive associations with treatment response. TMB had the highest correlation (τ = 0.30), while PDCD1 and GEP showed weaker associations (τ = 0.21, τ = 0.22).

Despite statistical significance, the correlation coefficients indicate that all three associations are relatively weak, with TMB showing a modestly stronger association. Therefore, none of the biomarkers individually demonstrates a strong association with treatment response.

• Explain the biological information captured by each biomarker and discuss their relative strengths and limitations

**Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB)** measures the number of somatic mutations per megabase of tumor DNA. A higher TMB can increase the likelihood of generating neoantigens, which may be recognized by the immune system and trigger an anti-tumor response. Its main strength is that it provides an indication of the potential immunogenicity of a tumor; however, not all mutations generate immunogenic neoantigens, and TMB does not directly measure immune cell infiltration or activity.

**PDCD1 expression** measures the expression of the gene encoding PD-1, an immune checkpoint receptor primarily expressed on activated T cells that regulates immune responses. Its relevance is particularly important in the context of immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, as blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway can restore aspects of anti-tumor immunity. However, elevated PDCD1 expression alone cannot distinguish productive immune activation from dysfunctional or exhausted T cells.

**T-cell-inflamed Gene Expression Profile (GEP)** summarizes the expression of 18 immune-related genes involved in T-cell infiltration, cytotoxic activity, antigen presentation and interferon signalling. It therefore provides a broader representation of the immune state of the tumor microenvironment. Its main strength is that it captures multiple aspects of anti-tumor immunity rather than relying on a single gene. However, bulk gene expression cannot distinguish between different cell populations, and averaging standardized expression values may conceal differences between individual immune pathways.

Overall, the three biomarkers capture complementary aspects of tumor immunology: TMB reflects the potential for tumor antigen generation, PDCD1 reflects immune checkpoint activity, and GEP reflects the overall immune activity of the tumor microenvironment. Although TMB ranks the highest with treatment response in our analysis, all three associations were weak. Combining these biomarkers could therefore provide a more comprehensive characterization of tumor immunogenicity and immune activity than relying on any single biomarker.

## RQ3 — Biomarker comparison: discrimination and combination

The previous section establishes that all three biomarkers are associated with response. This section asks which of them discriminates best, whether they carry independent information, and whether combining them helps.

All three on a consistent basis: `log2(TPM + 1)` and RQ2's gene list. Because `PDCD1` is one of those genes, the score is rebuilt here without it. Each biomarker there is tested on every patient who has it measured; ranking them against each other needs one cohort, so the comparisons below use the 150 patients with all three values. That costs little: the GEP's AUC is 0.731 (0.619–0.833) on all 192 and 0.756 (0.643–0.855) on the matched 150, because precision is set by the 25 responders and only 4 of them lack TMB.

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-setup

clin3 <- as.data.frame(clinical)
clin3 <- clin3[match(colnames(tpm), clin3$sample_id), ]
stopifnot(identical(as.character(clin3$sample_id), colnames(tpm)))
clin3$BOR <- factor(clin3$BOR, levels = c("NR", "R"))

lt3 <- log2(as.matrix(tpm) + 1)
stopifnot(identical(df_rq2$sample, colnames(tpm)))   # GEP score from RQ2

# PDCD1 is one of the 18 genes in the exercise's list, so the score used here is
# rebuilt from the other 17 to keep it off both sides of the comparison. The
# correlation below shows how little this changes.
gep17_genes <- setdiff(intersect(gep_genes, rownames(lt3)), "PDCD1")
stopifnot(length(gep17_genes) == 17)
gep17 <- colMeans(t(scale(t(lt3[gep17_genes, , drop = FALSE]))), na.rm = TRUE)

cat("full 18-gene score vs 17-gene score (PDCD1 removed): rho =",
    round(cor(df_rq2$gep_score, gep17, method = "spearman"), 4), "\n")

bm <- data.frame(
  BOR   = clin3$BOR,
  PDCD1 = as.numeric(lt3["PDCD1", ]),   # log2(TPM+1), not raw counts
  GEP   = gep17,                        # 17 genes, PDCD1 excluded
  TMB   = clin3$TMB                     # mutations/Mb, from DNA
)
summary(bm)
```

### Missing TMB and complete-case analysis

TMB is missing for 42 patients, so check they do not differ systematically before dropping them.

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-missingness

miss_tab <- table(has_TMB = !is.na(bm$TMB), BOR = bm$BOR)
miss_tab

cat("response rate with TMB:",
    round(100 * miss_tab["TRUE", "R"] / sum(miss_tab["TRUE", ]), 1), "%",
    "| without TMB:",
    round(100 * miss_tab["FALSE", "R"] / sum(miss_tab["FALSE", ]), 1), "%\n")
cat("Fisher p (response vs TMB availability):",
    signif(fisher.test(miss_tab)$p.value, 3), "\n")
cat("GEP score differs by TMB availability? p =",
    signif(wilcox.test(GEP ~ is.na(TMB), data = bm)$p.value, 3), "\n")

cmp <- bm[!is.na(bm$TMB), ]
y3  <- cmp$BOR == "R"
cat("\ncomplete cases:", nrow(cmp), "| responders:", sum(y3), "\n")
```

*Patients without TMB do not differ in response rate or GEP score, so dropping them is unlikely to bias the comparison.*

### Discrimination of each biomarker

Wilcoxon per biomarker, then AUC with a bootstrap interval, which puts all three on one scale regardless of their units.

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-auc

boot_auc3 <- function(score, reps = 2000) {
  set.seed(42)
  replicate(reps, {
    ix <- c(sample(which(y3),  sum(y3),  replace = TRUE),
            sample(which(!y3), sum(!y3), replace = TRUE))
    auc_mw(score[ix], y3[ix])
  })
}

auc_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB"), function(v) {
  b <- boot_auc3(cmp[[v]])
  data.frame(biomarker = v,
             wilcox_p  = signif(wilcox.test(cmp[[v]] ~ cmp$BOR)$p.value, 3),
             AUC       = round(auc_mw(cmp[[v]], y3), 3),
             ci_lo     = round(quantile(b, 0.025), 3),
             ci_hi     = round(quantile(b, 0.975), 3))
}))
print(auc_tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

*All three separate responders from non-responders, with TMB ranking highest.*

A ranking means nothing unless the gaps exceed sampling noise, so the differences are bootstrapped directly.

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-auc-differences

pairs3 <- list(c("GEP", "PDCD1"), c("TMB", "GEP"), c("TMB", "PDCD1"))

do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs3, function(pr) {
  set.seed(42)
  d <- replicate(2000, {
    ix <- c(sample(which(y3),  sum(y3),  replace = TRUE),
            sample(which(!y3), sum(!y3), replace = TRUE))
    auc_mw(cmp[[pr[1]]][ix], y3[ix]) - auc_mw(cmp[[pr[2]]][ix], y3[ix])
  })
  data.frame(comparison   = paste(pr[1], "-", pr[2]),
             diff         = round(mean(d), 3),
             ci_lo        = round(quantile(d, 0.025), 3),
             ci_hi        = round(quantile(d, 0.975), 3),
             distinguishable = !(quantile(d, 0.025) < 0 & quantile(d, 0.975) > 0))
})) |> print(row.names = FALSE)
```

*Every pairwise difference straddles zero, so no biomarker is demonstrably better than another in this cohort.*

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-roc
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5

roc_pts <- function(score, lab) {
  o <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE); pos <- y3[o]
  data.frame(fpr = c(0, cumsum(!pos) / sum(!y3)),
             tpr = c(0, cumsum(pos)  / sum(y3)),
             biomarker = lab)
}
roc_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB"),
                                 function(v) roc_pts(cmp[[v]], v)))

p_rq3d_roc <- ggplot(roc_all, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = biomarker)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey65") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(PDCD1 = starfish[3], GEP = starfish[6], TMB = starfish[1])) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Discrimination of each biomarker", x = "False positive rate",
       y = "True positive rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p_rq3d_roc
ggsave("figures/RQ3D_roc_comparison.png", p_rq3d_roc, width = 5, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

### Independence of the three biomarkers

If two of them measure the same biology, ranking them is beside the point.

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-correlation

round(cor(cmp[, c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB")], method = "spearman"), 3)
```

*PDCD1 and the GEP measure nearly the same thing (ρ = 0.90); TMB is independent of both.*

### Combining the biomarkers

TMB is log-transformed as in RQ1, and all predictors are in SD units so the coefficients are comparable.

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-combinations

z3 <- cmp
z3$PDCD1 <- as.numeric(scale(z3$PDCD1))
z3$GEP   <- as.numeric(scale(z3$GEP))
z3$TMB   <- as.numeric(scale(log2(z3$TMB + 1)))

model_set <- list("PDCD1" = BOR ~ PDCD1, "GEP" = BOR ~ GEP, "TMB" = BOR ~ TMB,
                  "GEP + TMB" = BOR ~ GEP + TMB, "PDCD1 + TMB" = BOR ~ PDCD1 + TMB,
                  "GEP + PDCD1" = BOR ~ GEP + PDCD1,
                  "all three" = BOR ~ GEP + PDCD1 + TMB)

# Coefficients are fitted on the same 150 patients the in-sample AUC is read
# off, which flatters models with more predictors. Repeated stratified 5-fold
# CV gives each patient a prediction from a model that never saw them.
cv_pred <- function(fm, R = 40, K = 5) {
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(z3), R)
  for (r in seq_len(R)) {
    fold <- integer(nrow(z3))
    fold[y3]  <- sample(rep_len(1:K, sum(y3)))
    fold[!y3] <- sample(rep_len(1:K, sum(!y3)))
    for (k in 1:K) {
      m <- suppressWarnings(glm(fm, data = z3[fold != k, ], family = binomial))
      out[fold == k, r] <- predict(m, newdata = z3[fold == k, ], type = "link")
    }
  }
  out
}

set.seed(7)
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(model_set), function(nm) {
  m  <- glm(model_set[[nm]], data = z3, family = binomial)
  cv <- cv_pred(model_set[[nm]])
  data.frame(model  = nm, AIC = round(AIC(m), 1),
             AUC    = round(auc_mw(predict(m, type = "link"), y3), 3),
             CV_AUC = round(mean(apply(cv, 2, function(pr) auc_mw(pr, y3))), 3))
})) |> print(row.names = FALSE)

cat("\nLRT adding TMB to GEP:        p =",
    signif(anova(glm(BOR ~ GEP, z3, family = binomial),
                 glm(BOR ~ GEP + TMB, z3, family = binomial),
                 test = "Chisq")$`Pr(>Chi)`[2], 3), "\n")
cat("LRT adding PDCD1 to GEP+TMB:  p =",
    signif(anova(glm(BOR ~ GEP + TMB, z3, family = binomial),
                 glm(BOR ~ GEP + PDCD1 + TMB, z3, family = binomial),
                 test = "Chisq")$`Pr(>Chi)`[2], 3), "\n")
```

*GEP + TMB is the best model on both AIC and cross-validation, and PDCD1 adds nothing once the GEP is included. Cross-validation separates what the in-sample AUC hides: all three drops to 0.809, below both pairs, and GEP + PDCD1 falls to 0.723, worse than either gene alone. Pairing two measures of the same axis costs a parameter and buys nothing.*

```{r}
#| label: rq3d-combination-roc
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5

# Out-of-fold predictions averaged over the repeats, so these curves are
# directly comparable to the single-biomarker curves above.
set.seed(7)
cv_roc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("GEP", "TMB", "GEP + TMB"),
                                function(nm) roc_pts(rowMeans(cv_pred(model_set[[nm]])), nm)))
cv_roc$biomarker <- factor(cv_roc$biomarker, levels = c("GEP + TMB", "TMB", "GEP"))

p_rq3d_cv_roc <- ggplot(cv_roc, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = biomarker)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey65") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("GEP + TMB" = starfish[2], TMB = starfish[1],
                                 GEP = starfish[6])) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Cross-validated discrimination",
       subtitle = "Out-of-fold predictions, 5-fold CV over 40 repeats",
       x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p_rq3d_cv_roc
ggsave("figures/RQ3D_cv_roc.png", p_rq3d_cv_roc, width = 5, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

*The two independent axes together clear either one alone; the gain comes from adding TMB, not from adding a second immune marker.*

### Interpretation

All three are individually associated with response on the same 150 patients: PDCD1 AUC 0.758 (0.654-0.851), GEP 0.756 (0.648-0.853), TMB 0.792 (0.685-0.885), all Wilcoxon *p* \< 2 × 10⁻⁴.

None is demonstrably better than another. Every pairwise difference straddles zero (TMB − GEP = 0.035, CI −0.085 to 0.164; GEP − PDCD1 = −0.001, CI −0.060 to 0.055). With 21 responders the study cannot resolve gaps this small, so TMB ranks highest while remaining within the others' intervals.

PDCD1 and the GEP are not independent (ρ = 0.90), and this is not an artefact of `PDCD1` sitting in the gene list, since the score used here excludes it. Both measure the T-cell-inflamed axis, and PDCD1's two ligands (`CD274`, `PDCD1LG2`) remain signature members. TMB is independent of both (ρ = 0.09, 0.14).

So the three biomarkers reduce to two axes: an RNA immune axis and a DNA mutational axis. GEP + TMB is the best model (AIC 93.1, cross-validated AUC 0.820); adding TMB to GEP is decisive (*p* = 1.4 × 10⁻⁵) while adding PDCD1 on top contributes nothing (*p* = 0.86). This matches Mariathasan et al., who report response associated with a CD8 T-effector phenotype and, more strongly, with mutational burden.

Each has a different weakness. TMB captures antigenic potential but says nothing about whether the immune system engaged, and it is missing for 22% of patients. PDCD1 is cheap and directly tied to the drug target, but it cannot separate activation from exhaustion, and a single gene is noisier than an average. The GEP is more stable across 18 co-expressed genes, though like any bulk measure it cannot tell where the T cells are.

## RQ4 —  The influence of tumor purity on immune-related biomarker

How might differences in tumor purity influence the expression of immune-related biomarkers and their observed associations with treatment response?

Bulk RNA-seq measures a mixture of tumour, immune and stromal cells. Low purity sample contains more non-tumour cells (immune cells), therefore will show higher values of PDCD1 and GEP genes which are genes expressed by T cells. Purity could thus mask or inflate the associations found in previous questions.

Purity estimation approach:
- estimate purity with ESTIMATE
- check if it differs between NR and R and correlate with each of the biomarkers
- compare the biomarker-response association with and without adjustment


```{r}
# Align clinical data and expression (join everything by sample ID)
clin <- clinical |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(sample_id %in% colnames(tpm)) |>
  mutate(BOR = factor(BOR, levels = c("NR", "R")))

# Base R needed here: ESTIMATE takes a genes-as-rownames matrix
log_tpm <- log2(as.matrix(tpm[, clin$sample_id]) + 1)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(log_tpm), clin$sample_id))

clin |> dplyr::count(BOR)
```
*Note: There is an imbalance between the number of NR-167 and R-25 that may limit the test below*
```{r}

# GEP from RQ2 score; PDCD1 on log2(TPM + 1)
gep <- df_rq2 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(sample_id = sample, GEP = gep_score)

pdcd1 <- tibble(sample_id = colnames(log_tpm),
                PDCD1     = log_tpm["PDCD1", ])

# TMB is right-skewed: log2-transform (noteffecting Wilcoxon and Spearman)
markers <- clin |>
  transmute(sample_id, BOR, TMB = log2(TMB + 1)) |>
  left_join(pdcd1, by = "sample_id") |>
  left_join(gep,   by = "sample_id")
```

### Estimating tumor purity with ESTIMATE

ESTIMATE uses single-sample GSEA to for a 141-gene stromal signature and a 141-gene immune signature,and calculates ESTIMATE score which is their sum. Based on exercise 4 this score was converted to purity with a cosine formula that was calibrated on Affymetrix microarrays. On RNA-seq, purity is representing relative ranking of samples.

```{r}
est <- log_tpm |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter_common_genes(id = "hgnc_symbol", tidy = FALSE,
                      tell_missing = TRUE, find_alias = TRUE) |>
  estimate_score(is_affymetrix = FALSE) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(purity = cos(0.6049872018 + 0.0001467884 * estimate))

est |> summarise(across(purity, list(min = min, median = median, max = max))) # values should be within 0–1

# Join by sample ID
dat <- markers |>
  left_join(est, by = c("sample_id" = "sample"))

stopifnot(!anyNA(dat$purity))
```
Purity score in all the samples ranges between 0.29 to 0.96

### Does purity differ between response groups?

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(BOR) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_purity = median(purity))

wilcox.test(purity ~ BOR, data = dat) |> tidy()

p_purity <- ggplot(dat, aes(BOR, purity, fill = BOR)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_BOR, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Response", y = "ESTIMATE purity", title = "Purity by response") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Both respond groups contain approximately the same ammount of non-tumour tissue, median 0.65 for NR and 0.62 for R. (Wilcoxon p = 0.17)

### Does purity relate to each biomarker?

Spearman correlations of each biomarker with purity, and separately with the immune and stromal components. These show which part of "low purity" drives each biomarker.

```{r}
cor_tab <- expand_grid(marker    = c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB"),
                       covariate = c("purity", "immune", "stromal")) |>
  mutate(
    n    = map2_int(marker, covariate,
                    \(m, c) sum(!is.na(dat[[m]]) & !is.na(dat[[c]]))),
    test = map2(marker, covariate,
                \(m, c) cor.test(dat[[m]], dat[[c]],
                                 method = "spearman", exact = FALSE) |> tidy())
  ) |>
  unnest(test) |>
  dplyr::select(marker, covariate, n, rho = estimate, p.value)

cor_tab

p_scatter <- dat |>
  pivot_longer(c(PDCD1, GEP, TMB), names_to = "marker", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(purity, value, colour = BOR)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              colour = "black", na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_BOR) +
  facet_wrap(~ marker, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "ESTIMATE purity", y = NULL, colour = "Response",
       caption = "PDCD1: log2(TPM + 1); GEP: mean z-score; TMB: log2(mut/Mb + 1)") +
  theme_minimal()

p_scatter
```

*PDCD1 and GEP fall as purity rises and correlates most strongly with immune score rather than stromal score. TMB with p = 1.45e-01 is barely related to purity. The slight increasing trend seen in the plot is a measurement effect as DNA mutations are harder to detect with lower purity.*

### Biomarker–response association with and without purity

Logistic regression, with the biomarker and covariate scaled to SD units, so the odds ratio is per 1 SD increase. For each biomarker the crude and adjusted models are fitted on the same samples (TMB has missing values), so they can be compared. The likelihood-ratio test (LRT) asks whether the biomarker adds information beyond the covariate, as Mariathasan et al. did when comparing models.

Two adjustments:

- **Purity**: built from immune and stromal genes, so it partly contains the immune signal we want to measure (risk of over-adjustment).
- **Stromal score only**: removes dilution by stroma without removing the immune signal.

With only 25 responders, each model has at most two predictors.

```{r}
standardise <- \(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)

assoc <- function(m, adj) {
  d <- dat |>
    drop_na(all_of(c(m, adj))) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(c(m, adj)), standardise))

  fits <- list(
    crude    = glm(reformulate(m, "BOR"),         family = binomial, data = d),
    adjusted = glm(reformulate(c(m, adj), "BOR"), family = binomial, data = d)
  )
  base <- glm(reformulate(adj, "BOR"), family = binomial, data = d)

  lrt_p <- anova(base, fits$adjusted, test = "LRT") |>
    tidy() |>
    pull(p.value) |>
    dplyr::last()

  fits |>
    imap(\(fit, model) tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
           filter(term == m) |>
           mutate(model = model)) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(marker = m, adjusted_for = adj,
           n = nrow(d), n_R = sum(d$BOR == "R"), LRT_p = lrt_p)
}

assoc_long <- expand_grid(marker = c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB"),
                          adj    = c("purity", "stromal")) |>
  pmap(\(marker, adj) assoc(marker, adj)) |>
  list_rbind()

# Summary table: crude vs adjusted OR, % change in log-OR, LRT
assoc_tab <- assoc_long |>
  dplyr::select(marker, adjusted_for, n, n_R, model, estimate, LRT_p) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = estimate,
              names_prefix = "OR_") |>
  mutate(pct_change_logOR = 100 * (log(OR_adjusted) - log(OR_crude)) / log(OR_crude))

assoc_tab
```

```{r}
p_forest <- assoc_long |>
  mutate(model = if_else(model == "crude", "crude", str_c("adj. ", adjusted_for))) |>
  distinct(marker, model, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, marker, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("crude" = "grey30",
                                 "adj. purity" = starfish[3],
                                 "adj. stromal" = starfish[6])) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio for response (per 1 SD, log scale)", y = NULL,
       colour = NULL, title = "Biomarker–response association") +
  theme_minimal()
p_forest
```
*Adjusting for purity increases the log-OR of PDCD1 to 43% and GEP by 74%, while adjusting for stromal changes had a smaller increase effect 9% and 21%. All biomarkers remained informative beyond purity (LRT p ≤ 6 × 10⁻⁴). Low-purity samples carry both immune cell in favour of response, and stroma which is linked to non-response,so the crude associations partly cancel these out. TMB is almost unchanged (2-3%).*

### Residualise and re-test

We remove the part of each biomarker that is statistically associated with purity, then repeat the Wilcoxon test from RQ3 on what is left.

```{r}
resid_tab <- c("PDCD1", "GEP", "TMB") |>
  map(\(m) {
    d <- dat |> drop_na(all_of(m))
    d <- d |> mutate(resid = residuals(lm(reformulate("purity", m), data = d)))

    tibble(
      marker  = m,
      n       = nrow(d),
      n_R     = sum(d$BOR == "R"),
      p_raw   = wilcox.test(reformulate("BOR", m), data = d)$p.value,
      p_resid = wilcox.test(resid ~ BOR, data = d)$p.value
    )
  }) |>
  list_rbind()

resid_tab
```
*After removing the part explained by purity, all three differ between response groups. This agrees with the regression results and RQ2/3, purity does not explain the associations, for GEP the signal is clearer.*

### Summary figure

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
grid.arrange(p_purity, p_forest, p_scatter,
             layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 3)))

ggsave("figures/RQ4_purity_summary.png",
       arrangeGrob(p_purity, p_forest, p_scatter,
                   layout_matrix = rbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 3))),
       width = 12, height = 8, dpi = 300)
```
*Summary of RQ4: top left - purity by response, top right -crude and purity- or stroma-adjusted odds ratios per SD, bottom -each biomarker against purity, coloured by response. Adjustment does not weaken the immune biomarkers, while TMB is unaffected.*

### Discussion

##### Why purity matters in bulk RNA-seq?

Lower purity means more non-tumour RNA in a sample. Since PDC1 and most of the GEP genes come from immune cells, a sample with lots of them will score high, while a sample with a lot of stroma gets diluted. So biomarkers tells us partially how much non-tumour tissue was sampled an not how inflamed the tumor is

##### Could purity explain the RQ2/RQ3 results?

Not really, all three biomarkers stayed associated with response after adjustment for purity, both with logistic regression and residual approach. For PDCD1 and the GEP the association actually got stronger. In the crude analysis stroma associated with non response nad immune cells associated with response partly cancel out so the immune signal may be underestimated. In Mariathasan et al., TGF-β-rich stroma keeps T cells away from the tumour, so low purity can mean either an inflamed or an excluded tumour.


##### TMB 

TMB comes from DNA sequencing, not RNA, so tissue composition barerly changes its association with response, in low purity TMB may be harder to detect so the measured values may be underestimated.

###### Would adjusting for purity improve the biomarker interpretation?

Not necessarily. In our data the adjustment improved the interpretation of GEP and PDC1 and their association with response, adjusting for stroma pointed the same way. However ESTIMATE purity is computed partly from immune genes, so adjusting the GEP for it is circular and can remove exactly the real T-cell signal. ESTIMATE purity on RNA-seq is an approximation, with no pathology or DNA-based estimate to validate it. With 25 responders the adjusted odds ratios are imprecise, so crude and adjusted results should be reported together.
  
##### What could be done better?

Oher analysis alternatives include cell-type deconvolution (e.g. quanTIseq, CIBERSORTx) and spatial immune phenotypes (inflamed, excluded, desert), as in the paper, would let us separate the immune and stromal effects more directly than a single purity number.
